direct_answer: BASF states it conducted a double materiality assessment “in accordance with the ESRSs” for the first time in 2024, building on prior assessments but increasing granularity and documentation, and explicitly assessing “potential and actual material impacts, risks and opportunities” at Group level “along our value chain” with stakeholder inputs and expert validation [Source 10]. BASF also explains that, due to methodological changes (more in-depth ESRS subtopic/sub-subtopic analysis and an added level of granularity using potential/actual IROs), its previous assessments are only comparable to the 2024 assessment at the highest abstraction level (topic level), though it reports a “high degree of correlation” at that level and found no entity-specific topics beyond ESRS-defined topics in 2024 [Source 12]. BASF’s approach includes (i) compiling potential sustainability matters relevant to its business, customer industries, and stakeholder groups with attention to higher-risk value-chain areas [Source 10]; (ii) incorporating direct and indirect stakeholder input (e.g., advisory councils, civil society forum, multistakeholder networks, and big data analyses of customer/capital market interests) [Source 10]; and (iii) identifying/validating risks and opportunities linked to impacts and dependencies using in-house experts and selected stakeholders (Nature and Human Rights Advisory Councils), leveraging its Group-wide opportunity and risk management [Source 10]. BASF reports outcomes consistent with double materiality, e.g., identifying material impacts/risks/opportunities for climate change [Source 8] and concluding ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users is not material due to its B2B model [Source 12].
compliance_rationale: Evidence shows BASF describes an ESRS-aligned double materiality process, including value-chain scope, stakeholder inputs, and integration with opportunity/risk management, and it explains comparability limits versus prior assessments due to methodological changes [Source 10] [Source 12]. However, the retrieved passages do not provide full detail on the impact materiality and financial materiality methodologies (e.g., criteria, thresholds, scoring) required to robustly evidence the double materiality principle beyond high-level process statements and selected results [Source 10] [Source 12].
disclosure_gaps: Detailed criteria/method for assessing impact materiality (e.g., severity/likelihood dimensions, how actual vs potential impacts are weighted) is not provided in the retrieved passages [Source 10] [Source 12].
Detailed criteria/method for assessing financial materiality (e.g., how financial effects are quantified/thresholded across time horizons) is not provided in the retrieved passages [Source 12].

Clear description of how impacts, risks and opportunities are mapped to specific levels of the upstream vs downstream value chain across all topics (beyond examples) is not fully evidenced in the retrieved passages [Source 10] [Source 11] [Source 15].
Governance/oversight specifics for the double materiality assessment process (roles, approvals) are not evidenced in the retrieved passages [Source 10].
Frequency is stated as planned annual updates, but evidence of the ongoing due diligence linkage/continuous process beyond stakeholder inputs is limited in the retrieved passages [Source 10].
key_findings: First ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment conducted in 2024; based on previous assessments but with increased granularity and documentation [Source 10].

Methodological changes mean prior assessments are only comparable to 2024 at topic level; BASF reports high correlation at that level and no entity-specific topics beyond ESRS topics in 2024 [Source 12].
Assessment performed at BASF Group level along the value chain; focused on higher-risk activities/sites/value-creation steps [Source 10].

Stakeholder interests incorporated via direct inputs (advisory councils, civil society forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect inputs (big data analyses of customer/capital market interests) [Source 10].

Risks and opportunities validated with in-house experts and selected stakeholders (Nature and Human Rights Advisory Councils) and linked to impacts and dependencies; draws on Group-wide opportunity and risk management [Source 10].
Example outcomes: climate change yielded multiple material impacts/risks/opportunities [Source 8]; ESRS S4 deemed not material due to BASF’s B2B model [Source 12].
